scoreNote: Strong (5): credits technology's real gains in reach, then argues it thins the depth of interaction and that its effect depends on use; sides with the first view as the more pressing truth while addressing both.

sentences.text: We have never been more connected, and yet complaints of loneliness have never been louder.

Some believe that our ever-increasing use of technology significantly reduces our opportunities for human interaction; others believe that technology gives us new and better ways to communicate and connect with one another.

Both views capture something true, but on balance the first is more persuasive: technology vastly expands the reach of our contact while quietly thinning its depth, so it tends to multiply connections even as it erodes the richest forms of interaction.
The optimistic view rests on undeniable gains.
Technology lets us speak instantly with people across the world, sustain friendships that distance would once have ended, and find communities of others who share our interests or our struggles.
A grandparent video-calls a grandchild on another continent, a patient finds a support group for a rare illness, and an immigrant stays close to the family she left behind.
For the lonely, the housebound, and the far-flung, these tools do not reduce interaction but create it where little was possible before.
For many people, then, technology has plainly widened, not narrowed, the circle of human contact.
However, this reach comes at a cost the second view overlooks.
The same devices that connect us across the world can pull us away from the people in the same room, as a family at dinner each disappears into a separate screen.
Digital contact tends to be more superficial than presence — a text is not a conversation, a click of approval is not friendship — and hours spent on screens are hours not spent face to face.
When shallow online exchange substitutes for deeper interaction rather than supplementing it, the quantity of contact rises while its quality quietly falls.
Technology can crowd out the very interaction it appears to provide.

sections.role: Body — It depends on how we use it

sentences.text: Moreover, the deeper truth is that technology is a tool, and its effect depends on how we use it.
Used to arrange a meeting, stay in touch between visits, or reach someone otherwise unreachable, it deepens human connection; used as a replacement for presence, it hollows it out.
The danger the first view names is real not because technology must isolate us, but because it makes shallow contact so easy that we drift into accepting it for the real thing.
The question is not whether the tool can connect us, since it plainly can, but whether we let it supplement our relationships or quietly replace them.
On current evidence, too often it replaces, which is why the first view's warning deserves the greater weight.
In conclusion, technology undeniably offers new and powerful ways to connect, yet it also tends to erode the depth of our interaction.

Because the gains in reach are so easily offset by losses in depth, and because the easy substitute so often crowds out the richer original, the first view captures the more pressing truth: our tools multiply contact while endangering genuine human interaction.
Let technology carry us to one another, not stand in for being there.
